My name is Spilla Franke. I work for the Jazz Archive at Tulane University, and I'm interviewing Frank Naundorf, who is from Berlin, Germany. The interview is going to be in German, mainly, except for some questions. This is February 25th, 1965. We're in the Barracks 27, the temporary quarters of the Jazz Archive now. Frank, how old are you?
I'm 24 years old.
Tell me how long you've been interested in the Jazz?
I came to the Jazz in 1954, by George Lewis's books.
Where did you find these books? I bought them in regular regular
And that was actually the beginning.
Are you there completely wrongly? Or have you ever heard American music?

Yes, so is that. We had a lot of American music in the radio. And then came the American bands back to Berlin. Big bands, hauptsächlich. Welche bands? Duke Ellington. I was not in those days. Lionel Hampton, Woody Herman, and Joseph at the Philharmonic. Louis Armstrong. Louis Armstrong. And then saw man natürlich the letters. And it was new. They were still young.
They were so 14, 15.
They were still younger.
And then they were still younger. And then they were still younger. They were still younger. Because it was a lot of young people. And then the flame was so over.
And you were suddenly very interested in the Jazz? Yeah, very interested. You noticed that was your music?

Yeah. But I noticed the difference between the albums I bought from Louis and the Big Band-Sachen, which I heard in concerts and in radio. And then was also Bill Haley very well. Was that not later? No, no.
That's right.
Bill Haley and Scum. Yeah, that was the beginning. And so far my money was reached, I bought me then only the plates. And then I had to do this Louis-Serie. And then I had to do this.
And then I had to do this. That were English? Or were those English?

No, they came out of the book. Where? That was the one who Bill Haley made in 1943. And then the Climax label. And then I bought me also Bank Johnson-Platten. And we had then also small groups. And then there was a couple of people who called it, like Gerhard Kowell.
Yeah, that's a Schlagzeuger.
Yeah, yeah.
In Berlin.
And then there was a group of people who had a great group. And they were in the Cosa Strasse in Dahlem. And they also had in the Eierschale, in the Jazz-Lokal, and other people had a great group.
That was the Jazz Club Berlin?
Jazz Club Berlin, yeah.
Or had the Kowell also a new group?
No, no. It was all in the Eierschale in the club. And they had a lot of the Krach. And then over these meetings, then expanded that knowledge. And then asked others. And then heard the songs more.
When did you start playing music?
I bought my first instrument. I played guitar before. I think it was 1953. I played guitar in the game and 1955 I bought my first Posaune. And I...
Have you taken a few hours?
No, I have learned.
Did you read that?
No, I played a year for a while. So, I played myself.
So, after what?

After a while. After a while. After a while. I took my degree. Three months. And started reading. And then I started reading. And then I brought it to a small Etude to Mozart. But that didn't lie to me. And then I gave it again. And then I gave it again. And...
But you have enough enough foundation for the harmonies to understand. Not only after a hearing room.
Well, in the last few years, it was built out. And then... And then... And then... How much need to read to someone to read the pieces we knew from the plates.
Have you ever played for Jenike?
Yes, for Jenike.
In the house of the youth?
Yes, I didn't know what the events were, but then also the great events. The Sporthall and the great events were there, where thousands of people were there.
That were then the amateur festivals?

Yes, festivals and big events for Easter and Christmas events. Jazz festivals. Then some people have been crystallized, they took contacts, my friends and I and others. Then there were new circles, which had more the same interests. There were more groups that were interested in one or two or more.
And where were you interested in?
New Orleans Jazz. And we had in our group the Co., I and a few others.
Do you know any names of the musicians, who are now known as musicians? Yes.

There were Horst Papa Henschel, Trompeter, Peter Strohkorb and the musicians who were called Salty Dogs. Yeah. And Gursche Beiersdorf, who played the Clarinet. So many of them are also back then, who were also back then, who were also back then, who were back then, who were in a different direction, who were in a different direction. And then there were many years here.
Was it for you mainly to play music or to have success with music?
No, no, it was the joy of this music and playing music. And it was just a pleasure to play music, as we heard it on the plates.
But it was also a little bit of a thing to bring.
First of all, you had to be the instrument to be the instrument and to make it with this style and to make it with this style, so that you could play in this direction.
Do you still play?
Yes, I still play.
And... Do you still play?

Well, I don't have any engagements in Berlin in this sense. I practice at home. And I have to play in the summer now Straßenparades with a English cappella, the... a guest with a guest in Berlin in two weeks.
What kind of cappella was that?

Keith Smith and his Climax Chance Band from London. With his name I also very well known. And... They had now also a tourney with Elton Purnell in England. And Keith Smith, the 15th and 16th March here in New Orleans. He played in California with Elton Purnell's band as exchange. While he had the Daniel Rueber geholt, he played with his cappella in California in two weeks. And then he will come back here.
Where dear but I am operating the machine, which is incidentally a Tanberg Monorail tape recorder.
Alright, my name is Dick Allen. We got it.
We have looked at your musical career now. Now tell us about your wife. Your wife plays Banjo, if I understand.
When I was met with her, when I was first to meet her, she played guitar.
When was that?

1962. She was also interested in jazz, of course, had no big knowledge, and was interested in music. She was interested in music. She was interested in my collection and my knowledge. I was also interested in her, that she should change the instrument and instead of the guitar, that Benjo should be able to grab the instrument.
How long did you play Banjo?

Two years. And that she did then. She did not have a high-quality instrument, but it was a western instrument, a western instrument, but it was very good to practice and learn. Then I had her my music knowledge in puncto harmonie, and melodic and so on. What I did on the Posaune, I had to give her a message. She did a lot of progress.
And she played together?

We play together, at home, and she played together. She played publicly, she played with the Key Smith Climax Band from London, as they were in Berlin. She was a night after the band game, she was sick and played all the night. She played well and was really good. I didn't hear it, because I was at home. She was about the disease. But the band was really happy with her. And I was really happy with her. And of course, when you've never played with a drum, you don't have the routine like a professional player.
There's a very good mood to it, that the first time it's getting into it.
Yes, sure. But when you have enthusiasm and the things that's what I like to do, and the chapel is also in the same style, then that's fine.
That's fine. Now tell us why you are here, and since you've played with the idea, to go to New Orleans and to study there, to work in jazz?
Yes, so on and for sure that's always my wish. That's always a financial question.
You have a job, so to say?

I have a job. I work mainly as a painter, also a painter, and also other things, also some opportunities, things that are in this direction, what has to do with painting. And my wife also worked. She went to the night on the post, she sent the letters and postcards.
How old is your wife?
My wife is 20.
And you have a small son?
We have a 2-year-old child.
Yes, the one you brought with.

Yes, the one we brought with. Yes, we didn't want to leave it at home. And we decided to go to a half a year and then we took all the staff into work, to finance the trip, to finance the vacation here.
Where did you lived all the time? If you spent all your money with all of them?

Well, I mean lived with them very close to the house. We lived very close, very close. Otherwise we could not do that. We were always able to do that. That's always the reasonable numbers that went on for the trip and for the trip. I wanted to do a recording session but that didn't have enough to do that. But that didn't have enough to do that. And I'm convinced that when I come here next time, that I can do something in this direction. I hope so.
What did you do here? What was the...
Well, we wanted to first look at the whole thing from the city and the musicians, from whom we've been listening to years, we've listened to the books, and read books.
And that you wanted to see all of them personally?
Yes. I wanted to see all of them personally and hear them.
Have you known many musicians here? Yes.

I also had the opportunity to play with a few of them. So Punch Millers Band, Billy & Dee Dee, and Kit Howard's Band, and Sweet Emmas Band. And we were very friends with George Gaynor, the Band-Jus-Spieler. We were looking for him right now, as we came here, to take him to take a degree. My wife wanted to take a degree. And his knowledge was done. And that went well. He was very good. He was very happy, that he had from far away a lot of students. There were many of him already, from England and Germany. And he was a very nice person. And we learned a lot from him.
Have you heard Marvin Kimberl in Old Absent House?
Yes, I heard him at the afternoon. And the band was very good. Have you ever heard your expectations?
No. Have you ever heard your expectations? Or is it so, as you hoped it would have been? No.

It was more than I hoped. And it's of course different, if you can see the music and the music and the music and hear them and play them, than if you can hear them just on plates. It's definitely something different. You can experience it more with them, if you can sit there and hear them and see them.
Before you came here, did you find support? Did anyone interested you for? What was so on your heart? Or did the people have you for crazy?

Yes. Of course, I tried to do, because I originally wanted to take pictures, originally from musicians, who have been very few on plates until now. And there I had a round of writing, I spoke to all those people, from whom I believed that they were just interested in New Orleans Jazz. I also had a lot of success with that.
Financial success?

Yes, financial success. But of course, it was just a drop on a hot stone. And these people, they only came from the close friends. And all the people, musicians and so-called Jazz fans, who were always talking to them, they didn't have been called themselves, or they wrote me letters. And I also received some letters, from which I was very surprised and surprised. For example, I received a letter, and there was a letter, I said, I should have to let that be, and I should have to do it in Europe, in Germany, in Germany. There would be more than just in the United States than in the entire United States.
Who wrote that?

Yes, this letter I have just from one, that is the main speaker of the King Oliver direction in Germany. That is Dr. Abi Hübner from Hamburg, who wrote that. That is a very good trumpet. And his cell, they play in the Oliver direction. And there are also in Frankfurt, Oliver Benz, and this kind of, and also in Berlin. And they all belong to a company, which is called the Society for the New Orleans Jazz. And Mr. Hübner wrote, that he could not understand it, and that not only a birth certificate from New Orleans enough to make good music. And also this society that has a new Orleans Jazz, that has its main seat in Frankfurt, which was initially very excited for it, and that has then nothing more heard.
And what did you say about the Tuxedo Band? Oh, yes.

So, yes. He came then on the recording of the Young Tuxedo Band to talk and he said, King Oliver would have turned in the grave spiraling if he would have heard this ! Yeah, that is of course very sad, if we wanted to do that, and that we wanted to do that and that we would get such a brief and then get such a brief.

What do you think of the music that is played from the commercial side?
Well, it is at the moment quite a bit of jazz in Germany because of the twist and the rock'n'roll.
But there are many bands that are being played as jazz bands?

Yes, that with the jazz cappella has also been passed. It was at the end of the 50s, 56, 57, 58, 60, it was still passed. There are still a few in every bigger city, there are still a few cappella, which are jazz bands that are more or less good. There are good cappella and good individual musicians.

So, do you speak now about professional or young people? I remember when I went to school, the elementary school in the last years, there were all kinds of bands of young people who had been together. And I thought that this was a direct kind of movement and I thought that would continue to keep it. That was a great hobby, that you could start at a certain age and you could come together and play music.

In this direction has been developed. And the people, it was more or less high schoolers and students who went to their job, they had been able to play, because most of them didn't have the interest in that big. It was more or less a band that you had with. It was only the people who had more interest in it. And it was paid for money. The term amateur or professional is absolutely so. The people who were in the same place were lost. The borders can't be found. But in the last time, there were only one or two professional cappella, who do traditional jazz bands. In Berlin, the Spursity Stumpers.
They are already old people. Yeah, they are always young.

They are always young. But they do, I mean, it has nothing to do with New Orleans music. It is a mix between Dixieland and Mainstream. And it is now working a lot with electric things, with the connectors and the connectors.

Real 2. Frank Naugendorf interview. Real 2. Wir haben über die Dixieland und New Orleans Jazz Bands in Deutschland gesprochen. Ich möchte da noch einige Fragen stellen, die für unsere Leute hier von Interesse ist. Was für Bands spielen richtigen New Orleans Jazz in Ihrer Meinung nach? Gibt es das überhaupt in Deutschland?

Also meiner Meinung nach gibt es das nicht. Wir haben etliche Bands in den verschiedenen Städten, die hauptsächlich in die King Oliver Richtung einschlagen. In Frankfurt, in Hamburg, auch in Berlin. Und die eben großen Teil die alten Aufnahmen von King Oliver kopieren. Und das ist meiner Meinung nach nicht für den Sinn des New Orleans Jazz, dass man eben was für Note nachspielen sollte. Wenn man selbst spielt, dann hat man ja auch etwas zu sagen. Und man kann sich anleiten lassen, man kann von den Platten lernen, die Stilart. Und man sollte doch eben in diesem New Orleans Stil spielen, aber nicht irgendwie jemand kopieren.
Gibt es Ihrer Meinung nach irgendeine Band drüben, sagen wir mal ruhig in Europa, die so ähnlich klingt wie eine Band hier?
Ja. Also ist meiner Meinung nach Ken Coyle's Band und Keith Smiths Band und Barry Martins Band. Und ich glaube, in Deutschland haben wir in dieser Richtung...
Ist da ein Unterschied? Können Sie da einen Unterschied hören zwischen deren Musik und der Musik, die hier jetzt noch gespielt wird?

Natürlich ist es ein Unterschied. Ich meine... Vor allen Dingen wird sehr viel... In Europa wird viel schnelle, schnelle Sachen gespielt. Ich habe hier festgestellt, dass hier viele Stücke sehr langsam und langsamer gespielt werden. Also die Tempi unterscheiden sich zwischen den hiesigen Kapellen und drüben. Hier wird alles mehr relaxed gespielt und ruhiger. Und drüben hat man viele Kapellen, die eben sehr schnelle Tempi spielen. Das ist mir hauptsächlich aufgefallen.
Finden Sie, dass die von Ihnen erwähnten Bands Ken Coyle und so weiter doch noch eine gewisse Originalität haben? Oder kopieren die nun wieder die heutigen New Orleans Musiker?

Sicher, die hören natürlich die Platten, die es von den heutigen New Orleans Musikern gibt. Aber sie haben einen eigenen Stil von Ken Coyle hauptsächlich. Er hat... Das ist Ken Coyle auch. Wenn er nun mit diesen Leuten und mit diesen Leuten spielt, wenn er einen Wechsel hat in seiner Band, das ist immer der Ken Coyle Sound. Das ist typisch für ihn.
Ich möchte jetzt nicht Worte in Ihren Mund legen. Could you ask him to repeat that? I couldn't understand it all. I'm on the truck. Okay.
Können Sie das bitte nochmal wiederholen? Der Lastwagen war so laut. Man konnte wahrscheinlich nicht verstehen, was Sie eben gesagt haben über Ken Coyle.

Also ich bin der Ansicht, dass Ken Coyle einen eigenen Stil gefunden hat und dass seine Band eben, auch wenn sie besetzungsmäßig wechseln, unterworfen ist, immer nach Ken Coyle klingt. Das ist immer der Ken Coyle Sound.
Und doch ist es am nächsten dem Klang einer New Orleans Band. Am ähnlichsten. Ja.
Nur die heutige Ken Coyle Band hat eine leichtere Rhythmusgruppe, wie sie mal früher war. Das ist eben durch verschiedene Wechsel hervorgerufen in der Besetzung.
Würden Sie sagen, das klingt jetzt ein bisschen radikal, aber würden Sie sagen, es gibt keine New Orleans Musik außer in New Orleans?
Ja. Der Ansicht bin ich.
Und deswegen sind Sie hergekommen?
Ja.
Was ist Ihrer Meinung nach... Glauben Sie, dass nur schwarze Musiker guten Jazz spielen können? Und was sind so die hauptsächlichen Meinungen in der Beziehung in Deutschland?

Ja, also ich persönlich glaube, dass nicht, dass nur farbige Musiker guten Jazz spielen können. Aber ich glaube, dass nur schwarze Musiker eben hier nur Leans diese Art von Musik machen können. Auch wenn ich hier die weißen Musiker gehört habe, ist doch ein Unterschied. Ich habe nicht viel gehört, ich habe nur einige gehört, aber das ist ein Unterschied zu den Farbien.
Können Sie den Unterschied beschreiben?
Ja, schon im Ton, von der Tongebung her. Die weißen Musiker, die haben kein so starkes Vibrator, wie zum Beispiel die Farbien.
Und woran liegt das, glauben Sie? Haben Sie sich da eine Meinung gebildet? Es ist schwer zu sagen.
Schwer zu sagen, ja.
Denn die Musik, die hier gespielt wird, ist ja doch das Produkt von weiß und schwarz zusammen. Das ist ja nun nicht bloß die Musik der Schwarzen.

Sicher, aber zum Beispiel, ich möchte was vielleicht als Beispiel angeben. Ich habe den weißen Kornetisten Johnny Wicks gehört, der gefällt mir außerordentlich. Aber im Gegensatz zum DDP ist ein großer Unterschied. Beide spielen mit Feeling und Swing und Drive. Aber im Ton und vom Gefühl her ist es eben ein Unterschied. Man kann den weißen und den farbigen Musiker heraushören.

Haben Sie während Ihres Aufenthalts hier den Klang und auch die Schnelligkeit der Musik in verschiedenen Gelegenheiten verglichen? Zum Beispiel bei Beerdigungen, bei Paraden, in gewöhnlichen Konzerten, wie zum Beispiel im Preservation Hall. Finden Sie, dass die gleichen Musiker bei verschiedenen Gelegenheiten verschieden spielen?
Nein.
Sie finden, es ist überall die selbe Musik?
Es ist überall, ob das bei einer Beerdigung oder bei einer Parade ist oder in den Kitty Halls, dass die immer eben... Es ist nicht unterschiedlich. Ich empfinde mich als unterschiedlich.
Ich habe ihn... Asked ihm über Tempo in relation to that.

Yes, I did. And he doesn't think there's much difference. Ich habe hier eine kleine Frage an der Seite. Haben Sie davon gehört, dass in Deutschland auch Beerdigungen mit Musik vonstatten gehen sollen?
Nein, das ist mir nichts bekannt. Ich selbst habe es noch nicht erlebt.
Sie waren gestern auf einer Beerdigung und das war das erste Mal, dass Sie so etwas miterlebt haben.
Das ist eine einmalige Sache.
Um auf die Haltung der deutschen Jugend zurückzukommen, finden Sie oder glauben Sie, dass mehr Interesse für modernen Jazz herrscht heutzutage als für alten Jazz?

Ja, sicher. Die Freunde des modernen Jazz sind einer großen Überzahl. Und ich habe so den Eindruck, dass es... Viele junge Leute, die glauben, es gehört so zum guten Ton, wenn sie eben zu modernen Konzerten gehen. Und es ist auch wieder... Die Interesse ist natürlich... Es ist auch wieder etwas Masche dabei, wie auch in den... Vor Jahren bei dem Tradition-Boom, wie das am Aufstieg war. Und eben die wirklich Interessenten, die sind doch in einer kleinen Zahl. Und das... Und das... In großer Masse, dass du nimmst, dann doch bloß mitläufst.

Die gehen, weil man geht. Ja, weil man geht. Die Idee hatte ich vor ein paar Jahren auch schon. Glauben Sie, dass es jetzt weniger ernsthafte Jazz-Liebhaber gibt, als sagen wir mal vor sechs, sieben Jahren?

Nein, das glaube ich nicht. Ich glaube, dass... Die wirklichen Jazz-Liebhaber, die sind immer noch bei der Sache und die haben vielleicht auch andere Leute beeinflusst und dass die Leute, die sich dafür interessieren, dass die auch wirklich... sich eben dafür einsetzen.
Abschaffter mit beschäftigen.
Ja.
Ich will sort of... stay with it at this point.

Do you want some more questions? Yes. Do you have some questions? Did you ask him about the parade there and the younger musicians you heard in them? Such as the trombonist with the Jefferson City Puzzards or the tuba player with the Lions?
He didn't go to that parade, by the way, in the first one. No, I will.
Oh.
Haben Sie irgendwelche jüngeren Musiker hier gehört, die aber im alten Spiel, im alten Stil spielen?
Ja, das war auf der Lions Parade, der tuba-Spieler und den jungen kleinen Artisten, der da spielte, Lester Wright.
Was hielten Sie für den?
Evans Morrison was a tuba player. Oh, ja.
Sousaphone, right? Ja, die passen recht gut in die Sache und es ist erfreulich, dass ich hier in New Orleans doch junge Leute finde, die in diesem alten Stil spielen wollen.
Another question?
Ja, please.
Do his musicians have, as you're asking this, have one favorite who influences them? Or do they assimilate several styles? You know?
I think he sort of answered that in the beginning.
Yeah. This may be off the track, but you have the story about George Gaynor fixing up the banjo.
No, we don't.
Decorating it.
Ihre Frau hat doch bei George Gaynor Banjos Unterricht genommen. Ja. Sie haben da eine schöne Geschichte zu erzählen über den Banjo.

Ja. Erst hatte... Ja, er wollte ja ursprünglich das Instrument verkaufen und das, das ich dann wohl doch überlege, ist auch verständlich, der Mann hängt ja an dem Instrument und er hat dann eben anstelle dieses Verkauf, hat er ihr Instrument aufgearbeitet und verbessert, verbessert, den neuen Steg und noch so neue Teile eingebaut und hat es auch verschönt in seiner Art mit Abziehbildern. Das sieht ganz lustig aus.
Ich dachte, er wollte ihn ihr schenken.
Nein, nein, nein. Er wollte...
Er wollte ihn ihr verkaufen
und dann hätte sich das überlegt. Naja, aber für... Man könnte sagen, es wäre geschenkt gewesen. Ja. Es war nur eine kleine Summe, die es wert gewesen wäre.
Ja, man kann doch verstehen, dass er sein altes Instrument behalten wollte.
Did he put a jack of diamonds on her banjo? Ja. Also? Also? The same? Ja. The car? Oh, that's funny. Did she have any trouble communicating with Mr. Gaynor? Was there a language barrier?
Konnte Ihre Frau ihn gut verstehen?

Ja, also die ersten Male war es etwas schwierig, aber nachher war es wunderbar. Wir haben... Waren Sie immer dabei? Ja, ich war immer dabei. Weil es ja hauptsächlich sich um Harmonien und Noten und so weiter handelte. Und wir haben ihn sehr gut verstanden und er ist ein sehr guter Freund und wir schätzen ihn sehr und wir sind froh, dass wir eben seine Bekanntschaft machen konnten und dass wir von ihm sehr viel gelernt haben. Und er ist einer, vielleicht möchte ich sagen, der, der lebende Banjo ist, der heute noch eben spielt. Er hat das Instrument aus dem... aus einem... in seinem... Er hat es gehoben aus seiner Bedeutung heraus. Früher wurde es nur als Rhythmusinstrument benutzt und er hat viel Neues dazu gemacht, getan durch seinen Singletonen. Er spielt so eine Gitarre eigentlich. Ja, und auch harmonisch und er hat sehr viel in dieser Richtung getan.

Abgesehen von George Gielner, haben Sie noch irgendwelche Lieblinge unter den Musikern hier, die Ihnen besonders gefallen oder vielleicht auch unter den toten Musikern? Welches sind Ihre ganz besonderen Lieblinge denn?

Ja, einer meiner größten Favourites ist Punk Johnson. Und... Ja, meine... Also, mir gefallen alle, die ich bis jetzt gehört habe, selbst gehört habe, auf Platten. Also, ich bin von allen sehr eingenommen. Da ist keiner, von dem ich sagen könnte, der gefällt mir nicht.
Mhm.
Elmar Talbert, der Trompeter, der mit Louis gespielt hat. Ich glaube, einer meiner großen Favourites.

Wenn Sie nun jetzt wieder nach Berlin zurückkehren, glauben Sie, dass Ihre Reise hierher Ihnen in irgendeiner Weise geholfen hat? Ihnen, sagen wir mal, eine Art von Prestige einbringen wird, sodass Sie von nun an mehr in der Richtung erreichen können?

Ja, das glaube ich und das hoffe ich, dass ich meinen Freunden oder die es werden könnten, mit meinem Wissen und was ich gehört und gesehen habe, dass ich die dazu anleiten kann, eben sich für die Musik zu interessieren und dass sie sich dafür einsetzen.
Das klingt alles so schön, aber was meinen Sie mit sich für die Musik einsetzen?
Naja, das ist erstens... Haben Sie da irgendwelche
konkreten Ideen?

Ja, erstens sollte man versuchen, eben in echten Nuallins Musik zu spielen, wie man es eben auf dem, wie ich es hier gehört habe und auf den Platten hört, ohne natürlich zu kopieren und zweitens sollte man versuchen, Musiker, die noch nicht Gelegenheit hatten oder sehr wenig Gelegenheit hatten, dazu verhelfen, dass sie Platten machen können und dass sie dadurch einer größeren Zahl von Leuten zugänglich gemacht werden können. Und immer wieder darauf hinweisen, dass der Nuallins Jazz nicht tot ist, wie so viele Leute behaupten, dass er noch immer lebt und das auch noch weiterleben wird, dass natürlich die Musiker im fortgeschrittenen Alter sind und das doch eventuell mal die Entwicklung einen Abschluss hat. Das ist natürlich klar und gerade deshalb sollte man... Deswegen wollen Sie
so viele Platten wie möglich aufnehmen?
Ja, was ich kann und ich werde immer dafür arbeiten und hoffe, dass ich recht bald irgendwie in dieser Hinsicht das meinige dazu tun kann.

Glauben Sie nun, dass New Orleans Jazz die einzige mögliche Art ist, Jazz zu spielen oder überhaupt Musik zu spielen oder sind Sie tolerant gegen andere Stilrichtungen und finden Sie, die haben auch alle Daseinsberechtigung?
Das finde ich. Jeder soll das spielen oder soll sich für die Sache interessieren und einsetzen, die ihm am Herzen liegt.
Das finde ich gut, denn ich kannte in Berlin einige Puristen, die sagten, es gibt sonst nichts anderes.
Nein, man muss tolerieren, das ist ganz klar.
Und Sie hoffen, im nächsten Jahr wieder hierher zu kommen? Ich hoffe. Und eine Platte aufzunehmen?
Ja, das ist mein Wunsch.
Und Sie sind weiter gewillt dafür zu hungern?

Ja, das bin ich, damit freuen. Und ich habe auch mit George Geno gesprochen und ich möchte, wenn ich eine Aufnahme machen kann, möchte ich, dass er eben der Lieder ist und die Musiker sich aussucht. Wir dachten, wir hatten da schon drüber gesprochen, wir dachten da an seinen Freund, Alex Bigger, den Drummer und John Handy, den Altsaxophonisten und vielleicht Dolly Adams, die Pianistin und noch einige andere Leute, vielleicht getauert und Jim Robinson. Aber das ist noch in weiter Ferne, ich war da. Dann müssen Sie erst mal wieder
tüchtig schuften, bis Sie da
zu weit sind.
Ja,
bis erst mal alles wieder reinkommen.
Ich finde es sehr schön, dass es solchen Idealismus noch gibt heutzutage. Did you have any more questions? Did you get his favorites
on all instruments, all the different instruments?
No, he was very vague. He sort of likes everybody.
Oh, yeah, I see.

Ja, meint er wenig auf jedem Instrument Bevorzuge, ja, das kann ich sagen. Also John Handy, Jim Robinson als Posaunisten, Louis Nelson auch und Trompeter und Kit Howard ist mein favorite, Dede Pierce und Percy Humphrey und George Lewis und George Gano und Joe Butler und Slowdrag und Billy Pierce Piano und Cy Phrase und Drums Joe Watkins.
That's quite a long list of things. Turbo?
Oh, Tillmann, yeah. Weber Tillmann.
What about, did he go to Buster's ever? Oh,
ich war Buster's auf der Eindbauer. Okay.
It's the bar where the musicians go to, I just wonder.

Ach so, ah, it's the bar, nein, da war ich nicht. How many of them have you visited in the home? Ich war bei Keith Thomas zu Hause einen Nachmittag und er war sehr nett und er spielte uns seine erste Platte vor, die er für American Music gemacht hat, 1951, glaube ich, mit George Gano zusammen und wir hatten sehr nett unterhalten, er zeigt uns Bilder von seiner England-Tournee, von seiner Karriere. War sehr nett und nachher hat er uns mit dem Wagen noch zur Fähre gefahren, im Fährschiff. Und ich hoffe, dass ich, wenn ich zurückkomme und eine neue Band gründe, dass ich eventuell die Gelegenheit habe, ihn oder vielleicht irgendeinen anderen Musiker für ein oder zwei Wochen rüberzuholen und dass man vielleicht ein paar Konzerte machen kann in Westdeutschland auch und so den Leuten zeigen kann, dass eben nur Lienz doch noch gespielt wird wie eh und je und dass es noch nicht tot ist, wie in Deutschland eben die Meinung herrscht, dass 1917 mit der Schließung von Storyville, dass eben der in Wallinz auch aufgehört hat. Diese irige Ansicht, die herrscht in den meisten größten Kreisen und schwer dagegen anzukommen.
Did you go to any jam sessions of private parties or anything?
Waren Sie auf irgendwelchen privaten parties und jam sessions? Nein, wie sind Sie überhaupt hier an die Musiker herangekommen durch Preservation Hall? Sind Sie dort zuerst hingegangen?
Ja, dort und zu Game Hall sind wir gleichzeitig hier.
Den haben Sie selbst aufgesucht und gefunden?
Wie
haben Sie ihn gefunden? Ich
bekomme die adresse von Mrs. Jaffee.

Oh. bamboo How has it been in the last years? Do you find more radio programs about the right Jazz in Germany and also TV-sendings? In my time, it is now 6 or 7 years ago, when I was interested in Jazz, you had to stay very early to have a Jazz-sendung to hear.

Is that still so? The Jazz-sendings are very late, mostly around 10.00, and have probably not been in the last few years. It's been television-sendings from the Behrendt, from the South Westfunk, but that's not too often. And otherwise, these two institutions are not as active as they could be.
Maybe it would be a way to do more for you, to do more for the New Orleans Jazz?

Yes, I have a friend of mine, Ria Sin, I wrote recently, who has a new club, also a new radio-send, Club 18, John Hendrick, and he has also some cappes from England to his Jubilations-sendings. Maybe it can help you to make a new festival in the next festival that a New Orleans-Musica can play. Maybe I can in this regard with him a new event. I hope.
That would be nice. I think the youth in Germany, in Europe, is more than the people here.
Yes, this capacity capacity is there. And when someone comes, who has really an alarm,
that's what's sad.
It's all screaming at all. So, capacity capacity is there. But you have to push them in the right way.
You could have to push them in the right way. That's very nice.
But in the future of this growth increase, the interests have been very on the material side and the interest of a music direction has been then back to the music direction.
I think that's it.
Thank you very much for having us so much told you. I wish for your archive and your work and your work and much success in the next few years.
Thank you. And we wish you very much success. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Okay, go ahead.
Ask him the question again.
Ask him the question again.
Ask him the question again.
What do you think of the different music places here in New Orleans? Have you seen the differences in the difference?

Also, I myself was only in three places. That was Preservation Hall, Dixieland Hall and Absinthe House. I was not in the paddock, because it was for me first to expensive. And since you can hear the music from outside and I also know who plays, I just hold for the cappella just for the trumpet. I just hold for the trumpet and Albert Burbing, the small artist, for the rest of the band. I don't like the band. I don't like the band. The Narwin Kimball Band in Old Absinthe House, the band has me very good. They are of course not so out of itself. They play quite dampened and loud. Maybe it is also the case that it is also a night local. And that it is not so that it is not so that it is not so that it is possible to get out of the crowd. And that it is also connected with sound. And that it is perhaps that the people will get out of the crowd. And sometimes it doesn't like it. I don't know. At any point, the cappella came a little dampened. But otherwise it was good. At Dixieland Hall, the band is also been ! You can hear from the musicians, from this group of musicians, the musicians play, modern influences, modern phrases. For example, by the Posaunists, Walden Fox Joseph, the band has been playing quite modern things. And I have also noticed that the band of the house tried to play the musicians only the things that they played on the Nobility Record Platten. And it is always called a requested number. And I think that his musicians cook with, like you say, dead. Maybe they don't want to play that. That it is busy. That they bring the band to the man. And they also floris. And the preservation hall? The preservation hall has liked me the best. Because the atmosphere is familiar there. And you feel like at home. And the music is all very relaxed. Plus I expected to hear different bands. And it was always like the same people. And it was always like the same people. And it was originally thought that more musicians can play there. But it has enjoyed me very well. And I'm going to go on. That is a project in your sense? Yes, that is a project in my sense. Yes.
Thank you very much. I think that's it. The paper is running out anyway.
Okay, I think that is it. We're... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Opening and introduction of Frank Naundorf
segments.summary: Dick Allen sets up the microphone; Spilla Franke introduces the interview, date, location and Naundorf's age.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Discovering jazz in 1954 through George Lewis books and American bands
segments.summary: Naundorf came to jazz in 1954 through books about George Lewis, plus American radio and big bands visiting Berlin.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Buying Louis Armstrong records and Bill Haley
segments.summary: Teenage enthusiasm; he distinguishes Louis records from big-band sound, mentions Bill Haley, and buys records as money allows.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Record labels and the Berlin jazz club scene at the Eierschale
segments.summary: Records from the books, Johnson records, small groups, Gerhard Kowell, and the Jazz Club Berlin at the Eierschale.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Learning guitar and trombone
segments.summary: He played guitar from about 1953, bought a trombone in 1955, taught himself, tried lessons and learned pieces from records.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Playing at youth events, amateur festivals and New Orleans circles in Berlin
segments.summary: Playing for Jenike at the youth house and big festivals; forming circles around New Orleans jazz with named Berlin musicians.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Motivation for playing and current activity; Keith Smith visit
segments.summary: Playing for joy, practicing at home, and an upcoming street parade with Keith Smith's Climax Jazz Band.

segments.chapter: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
segments.title: Dick Allen explains the recording machine
segments.summary: Technical aside about the Tandberg tape recorder.

segments.title: His wife learns banjo and plays with Keith Smith's band
segments.summary: He met his wife in 1962, steered her from guitar to banjo, taught her harmony, and she sat in with the visiting band.

segments.title: Financing the trip to New Orleans
segments.summary: His wish to study in New Orleans; his painting job, wife's post office work, and bringing their child.

segments.title: Meeting and playing with New Orleans musicians; banjo lessons with George Guesnon
segments.summary: He wanted to meet musicians in person; sat in with several bands, befriended Guesnon, heard Kimball; it exceeded expectations.

segments.chapter: Reception in Germany and Berlin scene
segments.title: Fundraising letters and Hübner's criticism of the Young Tuxedo Band
segments.summary: Fundraising by letter had modest success; Dr. Hübner of Hamburg wrote that New Orleans birth does not guarantee good music, criticizing the Young Tuxedo recording.

segments.chapter: Reception in Germany and Berlin scene
segments.title: Brass band parade in Berlin with Keith Smith's band
segments.summary: In 1963 Berlin friends and the English band organized a street parade; police stopped it for lack of permission.

segments.chapter: Reception in Germany and Berlin scene
segments.title: German jazz scene, commercialism and decline of amateur bands; tape change
segments.summary: Commercial pressure, twist and rock, fewer jazz bands, and professional traditional bands in Berlin; reel ends.

segments.title: Reel 2 opening
segments.summary: Reel 2 begins; Franke switches to German and asks about authentic New Orleans bands in Germany.

segments.title: German and British bands versus New Orleans, and the Ken Colyer sound
segments.summary: Bands copying King Oliver; Colyer, Smith and Martin bands; faster tempi in Europe; Colyer's own sound.

segments.title: Whether only Black musicians play New Orleans music; tone differences
segments.summary: He believes New Orleans music belongs in New Orleans and hears differences in tone and vibrato between white and Black players.

segments.title: Funerals, parades and concerts: same playing everywhere
segments.summary: He finds no difference in playing across occasions; funeral music is unknown in Germany; he attended his first funeral the day before.

segments.title: German youth interest in modern versus traditional jazz
segments.summary: Modern jazz fans outnumber traditional ones and many go as fashion; serious fans remain.

segments.title: Young musicians in the Lions parade
segments.summary: Younger players in the old style, including a tuba player and Lester Wright.

segments.title: George Guesnon fixes up the banjo and teaches his wife
segments.summary: Guesnon refurbished and decorated the banjo instead of selling it; lessons went well despite language; his role as banjoist.

segments.title: Favorite musicians: Punch Miller and Elmer Talbert
segments.summary: He likes everyone but names Punch Miller and Talbert.

segments.title: Plans after returning home: promoting New Orleans jazz and recording
segments.summary: He hopes to promote the music, help musicians make records, and return to New Orleans to record.

segments.title: Planned recording with George Guesnon as leader
segments.summary: He plans a recording led by Guesnon with named musicians if he can return.

segments.title: Favorite musicians by instrument and visiting Kid Howard at home
segments.summary: A list of favorites on each instrument, missing Buster's, and an afternoon at a musician's home; plans to bring one to Germany.

segments.title: How he found the musicians in New Orleans
segments.summary: He went to Preservation Hall and Dixieland Hall and got an address from Mrs. Jaffe.

segments.title: German radio and TV jazz programming and closing thanks
segments.summary: Jazz broadcasts late at night; a friend's radio club; the potential for youth interest; thanks.

segments.title: Comparing New Orleans venues and sign-off
segments.summary: He compares Preservation Hall, Dixieland Hall and the Old Absinthe House; the recording ends.
